extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural students, builders, and informed general readers interested in Gothic/venetian arch design and masonry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for designing, assessing, and constructing masonry arches (forms, voussoir geometry, cusps, keystones, and masonry backing), with examples drawn from Gothic and Venetian practice. Emphasizes structural principles (line of resistance, joint geometry, scale/masonry interaction) and aesthetic/constructive tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arch line (ghost) and line of resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'arch line' is the ghost or skeleton (the spinal marrow) of the arch; its structural character is the 'line of resistance'. The architect must conceive and shape this line, opposing adverse forces which try to distort it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the line of resistance is kept within the voussoirs (preferably centrally). If the line approaches the edge of the voussoirs the arch is in danger; if it emerges out of the voussoirs the arch will fall. Use voussoirs and other constructive elements as 'armor' to guard and keep the line to its duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible arch line versus structural line
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two arch lines: (1) the visible direction/curve (apparent conduct) and (2) the line of resistance (true stability). The visible curve may have little to do with the real stability of the arch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that visible form and structural stability may differ; when classifying or arranging arches use the visible line (because the line of resistance varies with load), but in construction ensure voussoirs are wide enough to include whatever the structural line is under expected loading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer circular arcs for ordinary work
rubrics_metrics.description: Good architects have generally been content with 'God's arch' — the arch of the rainbow (circular arcs such as semicircle, horseshoe) — as the most useful and beautiful for ordinary work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid eccentric forms (elliptical, four‑centred, other singularities) for general architecture. Reserve complicated curves for specialised engineering where backing/bearing conditions justify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reversed internal curves on gables at large scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Arches formed by reversed curves on the inside of the gable weaken the external curve's benefit and have a natural tendency to dissolve under their own weight; on a large scale they are features of 'detestable ugliness' and instability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use reversed internal curves as principal large-scale arrangements. They may be tolerable in small scale or with specific allowable modifications (e.g., some roof details), but are inappropriate where structural solidity is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective use of ogee/double curve
rubrics_metrics.description: The double curve (Ogee) has a high aesthetic value and occurs in many traditions, but its varieties are infinite and its safety depends on masonry and scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ogee profiles are admissible and desirable when the scale and masonry render them secure (or when they harmonize with well-managed arches below). Avoid large-scale application where they become 'barbarous'; always ensure backing/masonry is appropriate for these capricious forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: arch versus excavation (when arch theory applies)
rubrics_metrics.description: An arch is a curved shell of firm materials carrying a burden of loose materials above; if the material above coheres (e.g., a solid rock), the opening is an excavation, not an arch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply arch theory only when the load above behaves like loose material (sand, gravel, rubble, water). Do not design as if an arch is needed where backfill cohesion will carry itself (e.g., tunnels in solid rock).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize voussoir thickness by line arrangement (not uniform thickening)
rubrics_metrics.description: The builder's problem is to carry the weight with the least thickness of shell; simply making every voussoir thicker is wasteful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thicken selectively where stress demands (commonly at the top). Use line- and shape-arrangement to distribute loads efficiently rather than uniform over-thickening. When necessary, add thickness at base or employ other expedients to avoid raising the arch unduly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent lateral spreading via targeted loading or internal thickening
rubrics_metrics.description: If an arch tends to burst in at the top it must consequently push out at the sides. Preventing the arch from starting out at critical side points prevents failure at the top.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, load the arch at the side points to resist thrust. If external loading is impossible (openings above, side position), hang or thicken weight under the arch (thicken shell inside) to resist lateral thrust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cusps — purpose, form, and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Cusps are added projections (the 'soul and life' of the best northern Gothic) that give inward weight to flank stones and draw them against the keystone. The true cusp is single; multiplication degrades dignity and usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a single well-placed cusp to provide inward weight and restraint. Be cautious of multiplying cusps (common degeneration in later Tudor work). Place and depth of the cusp should vary with direction and magnitude of the load, though often determined by aesthetics; recognize families (down-, mid-, up-cusped) and select per structural need and appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mont-Cenisian (monolithic/backed) masonry permits different treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: When the masonry above an opening is colossal and granitic (Mont‑Cenisian), the arch form matters little because the backing carries itself; examples include arches cut into single blocks or massive masonry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where massive backing exists, you may employ varied and even fanciful arch profiles because the backing handles the loads. Conversely, where only the thin arch shell must carry loose fill, adhere to arch principles carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voussoir count and joint placement rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Three pieces is the smallest number showing the essential arch principle and is representative of arch masonry. For pure circular or pointed arches the number/placement of joints matters less, but for bizarre forms (e.g., ogee) joint positions must be particular and masonry simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt three-piece (or suitably ordered multi-piece) masonry as the archetype for reliable arches. For complex curvatures keep joints simple and specifically placed; do not increase joints indiscriminately in capricious profiles unless masonry and technique allow it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keystone form affects strength and appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting different keystone profiles changes strength and aesthetics (e.g., r-form vs s-form); some keystone shapes are weaker but adequate when material (good marble) and thickness are sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select keystone shape considering material strength, scale, and backing. Changes in keystone design evolved experimentally; choose forms that balance desired appearance with demonstrated structural adequacy for the intended scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy by composite construction (stone cut away, brick backing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portions of carved marble (e.g., side pieces with cusps) may be cut away and replaced with bricks behind; if properly backed by brickwork this composite can be just as strong as full-stone construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use composite marble-and-brick construction to economize or achieve particular profiles provided the backing is adequate and the overall masonry remains sound. Recognize that such substitutions change the visual and constructive character and must be judged accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voussoir joint inclination and proportion principle
rubrics_metrics.description: In round arches joints are perpendicular to the curve. The natural arrangement is that each voussoir's outer and inner arched surface lengths be in the same proportion to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for joint geometry where inner and outer arched surface lengths of each voussoir are proportionate (or closely approximated), as enforced in the best Gothic buildings. This nicety improves structural performance and should be attended to in careful work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and masonry determine safety and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Many capricious or ornate arch forms (ogees, four‑centred) depend entirely for safety, fitness, and beauty on the quality of their masonry and on scale; built large or with many voussoirs they can be unsafe and absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always assess forms in light of scale and masonry quality. Reserve intricate or capricious profiles for scales and backing where they can be made secure; otherwise prefer simpler, proven forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shell shaping for vertical pressure (typical effective profiles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arches that bear vertical pressure perform better when their shell is shaped with internal thickening/projections (types b/d) rather than the simple thin shell (a). Projections (cusps) are central to northern Gothic solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt shell profiles that provide resistance to vertical loads (thicken at top or add internal cusps/projections). Use the typical forms (as illustrated) that have been used worldwide from antiquity to modern times as reliable templates for resisting vertical loading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization and practical carving practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Venetian practice suggests side pieces with cusps were carved in pairs (standard blocks) and adapted by beveling or turning to fit varied window widths; cusps were often carved entirely in the side pieces rather than carried into the keystone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor practical standardization where appropriate (paired side pieces, modular carving) to economize production and simplify ornamental work. Keep cusp ornamentation largely within side pieces so ornament can be executed without complex reference to each arch's keystone.
